extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP practitioners, and parties involved in civil patent litigation in the Republic of Korea
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and evidentiary rules, remedies, and court practices applicable to civil patent (and utility model) litigation in the Republic of Korea, including preliminary injunctions, evidence production, experts, trade-secret protection, trial scheduling, and ADR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction remedies and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: When granting a preliminary injunction, the court may prohibit the defendant from continuing manufacture or sale of the infringing goods, order that infringing articles or other articles used to infringe be transferred to the custody of a court bailiff, or instruct the bailiff to post public notice on the defendant’s premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A preliminary injunction may be enforced while an appeal or challenge is pending. The plaintiff is generally required to post a security deposit or bond to compensate the enjoined party if the injunction is later overturned; the deposit is returned when the injunction becomes final. The court has discretion to grant additional hearings before resolving the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security deposit and potential liability for improperly issued injunctions
rubrics_metrics.description: The court generally requires the plaintiff to post a security deposit or bond when a preliminary injunction is issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a preliminary injunctive order is later found to have been improperly issued, the right holder that petitioned may be liable for ordinary and reasonably foreseeable extraordinary damages, and is rebuttably presumed negligent in enforcing the injunction under Korean law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense of abuse of right in preliminary injunction proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant may raise a defense of abuse of right to avoid enforcement of a patent based on likely invalidity of the asserted patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although such a defense may avoid enforcement, the patent cannot be formally invalidated in a preliminary injunction proceeding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary evidence requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary evidence may include patent specifications, technical literature, published materials, patent gazettes, patent registers, and non-documentary items (products, models, photographs, videos) that help explain technical aspects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle, documentary evidence must be submitted in original copy, but scanned versions are acceptable in practice unless authenticity is disputed, in which case the nonconverted original must be available at trial. Any foreign-language document must be submitted with a translation (except permitted languages in international cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inspection (product or on-site) requests and standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Either party may request court inspection of samples of the other party’s products or on-site inspection of the other party’s property (e.g., manufacturing facility). The petitioner may request the court to order the other party or a third party to submit the product for inspection if they lack a sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petitioner must persuade the court that inspection is necessary (e.g., to prove infringement involving a manufacturing process). The court may inspect directly or appoint an expert to inspect and submit findings, and will often appoint an expert to accompany judges in manufacturing-process inspections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court-appointed expert evaluation: appointment, disqualification, and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The court may appoint independent experts to provide testimony on complex technical issues (Article 335 Civil Procedure Act) at a party’s request or on its own motion; it may also seek opinions from public institutions or foreign public institutions (Article 341).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party may petition for a specific expert, and the opposing party may object to that expert by showing bias or disqualifying grounds. The court has broad discretion to select or deny experts. Court-appointed experts must take an oath, may be subject to perjury penalties, and, if necessary, may enter a party’s premises with court approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document submission order under the Civil Procedure Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Article 343 (and related provisions), a party may petition the court to order another party or third party to submit a document relevant to the merits of the case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A petition (Article 345) must clearly indicate the document title, purpose, the person holding it, the facts it proves, and the legal basis for production. The holder has an obligation to produce if: (i) they are a party and have referred to the document in the lawsuit, (ii) the petitioner is legally entitled to demand delivery/perusal, or (iii) the document was made for the petitioner’s benefit or concerns their legal relationship, subject to statutory exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material submission order under the Patent Act (scope and consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act expands submission orders from 'documents' to 'materials,' which may include electronic files, video clips, and other nondocumentary data, and enhances consequences for noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The amended law prevents parties from simply refusing on trade-secret grounds; the petitioning party should first establish (in camera if necessary) that the materials contain trade secrets. The holder may request limited disclosure or restrict who can access materials. If materials are withheld without justification, the court may presume the petitioning party’s contentions based on the materials are true. The amendment applies to infringement actions filed on or after June 30, 2016.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accused infringer’s evidentiary obligation after prima facie showing
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginning July 9, 2019, accused patent or utility-model infringers must respond to credible (prima facie) infringement claims with evidence rather than simple denials when evidence of infringement is largely in the defendant’s possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prima facie showing of likely infringement is made and the accused denies infringement, the accused must present evidence of the actual process or product it practices or risk the court presuming that the accused infringing activity occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence preservation (pre-litigation or during litigation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence preservation is a tool to obtain evidence otherwise difficult to secure. Petitions to preserve evidence have been granted in some patent infringement cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To succeed, the petitioner should establish a likelihood or reasonable probability of patent infringement and the necessity of preservation. A successful order will state that evidence examination shall be conducted and that the respondent is ordered to submit materials; the annex will specify the subject, place, date of examination, facts to be proven, and subject materials. Petitions may be filed before filing the infringement action (to the district court having jurisdiction over the party or evidence location) or after filing (to the court where the lawsuit was filed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witnesses (substantive focus and procedural steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert witnesses in patent cases testify on technical issues such as the level of ordinary skill in the art at filing, prior-art disclosure, analysis/comparison of accused goods, loss caused by infringement, and reasonable royalty amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To call an expert, the petitioner must submit a 'Basic Statement for Expert Witness' (forms available in court practice directions). Expert opinion may be submitted via declaration (more common) or direct testimony at trial upon request; questions to be asked must be submitted in writing prior to trial. If testimony is allowed, the opposing party can cross-examine; cross and redirect questions need not be prefiled. The court may also appoint experts to evaluate disputed technologies or damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial technical examiners and technical advisors: roles and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Court has full-time judicial technical examiners (often dispatched from KIPO) and judicial technical researchers with scientific/technical expertise to support dispute resolution; the court may also appoint external technical advisors from a registered pool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial technical examiners help the judicial panel by providing technical explanations, participating in preparatory hearings, conducting technical explanatory sessions for judges, and may participate in trials with permission. Technical advisors submit written opinions or attend trials to explain technical matters and are bound by confidentiality and treated as government employees for certain criminal-law purposes. Judicial technical examiners normally are court employees; technical advisors are appointed case-by-case from external experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical explanatory and technology review sessions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial panels hold internal technical explanatory sessions (pre-trial, judges only) with judicial technical examiners to understand relevant technologies; on the trial date, technology review sessions allow parties to present and explain technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pre-trial explanatory sessions judges are educated internally with neutral court technical examiners; in technology review sessions parties or counsel present materials (drawings, products, videos) and are advised to submit materials prior to trial (PDF/slideshow/video) which become part of the court record. Sessions may be held in foreign languages with consent and court approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited access to trade secrets in litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Access to portions of the court record containing trade secrets may be restricted by court order so that only the parties to the lawsuit may access or copy those portions, or the court may require delivery of authentic/certified copies or abstracts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such restricted access cannot by itself prevent a party from divulging the trade secret to others; confidentiality protective orders (see below) are used to limit dissemination more broadly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality protective orders for trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: A party may petition for a confidentiality protective order when documents to be produced contain trade secrets; the court may conduct an in camera review and issue an order restricting use and disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The petitioner must establish that the submitted or to-be-submitted material contains trade secrets and that its use/disclosure outside the litigation would likely impede business operations; the petition must specify the persons to be subject to the order and identify the trade secrets. Orders may prohibit use/disclosure beyond the litigation (including cross-use in other suits domestic or foreign). Violation can lead to criminal punishment (up to five years imprisonment or a fine up to KRW 50,000,000), enforceable only after a complaint is filed by the petitioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective measures when court orders submission of documents/materials
rubrics_metrics.description: When the court orders submission of documents or materials to decide production obligations, it must take measures to protect the document from disclosure to others (e.g., in camera review, sealed handling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material submission orders under the Patent Act likewise require safeguards when materials withheld are ordered for review; the court will review in camera so the materials remain sealed from the other party or third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trial scheduling and process in civil patent lawsuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Civil patent trials typically involve a series of oral-argument dates spaced three to five weeks apart, with the court rendering decision in three to four weeks after the trial is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First trial date identifies disputed issues and holds technology review; subsequent dates focus on remaining issues, evidence examination, and witness examination. At each date the court schedules the next date and notifies issues to be addressed; parties submit briefs and evidence in advance of each scheduled date. The court decides whether it has heard enough to render a decision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement in litigation: process and legal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A settlement in litigation refers to an agreement reached before the judge during pending litigation by mutual concessions on claims at issue; it has the same effect as a final and conclusive judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In principle, a settlement in litigation must be stated verbally in court on a hearing date to be recorded; it can also be constituted if one party authenticates intent to settle in a brief and the other accepts in court. A settlement in litigation closes the lawsuit, the record has executory force for compulsory execution, and produces res judicata consequences (nullity claims are limited and require revocation procedures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Court settlement recommendation and its effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A court, commissioned judge, or entrusted judge may ex officio render a ruling recommending settlement to fairly settle the case, taking into account parties’ interests and circumstances within the claim’s gist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ruling of settlement recommendation has the same effect as a judicial settlement when neither party raises an objection within two weeks of receiving the ruling (or the objection is withdrawn/waived).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mediation institutions, proceedings, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Mediation is judicial ADR where a neutral third party intervenes to help parties settle; mediation can be conducted by mediation judges, standing commissioners, mediation councils, the court handling the lawsuit, or entrusted external institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mediation can be initiated by a party filing a request or by court referral; proceedings usually occur in a court mediation chamber but may be held elsewhere, may be sealed, and conclude when the agreement is recorded. A mediation record has the same effect as a judicial settlement; if mediation fails the case proceeds (or returns) to litigation. A mediation judge may render a 'ruling in lieu of mediation' (mandatory mediation ruling) that has the same effect as a judicial settlement unless objected to within two weeks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arbitration characteristics compared to litigation and mediation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arbitration is a private resolution by award of an arbitrator rather than a court judgment; it is nondisclosed in principle, procedurally more flexible, and typically single-instance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arbitration shares features with litigation (reasoned award, similar finality) but differs from settlement/mediation in that the arbitrator renders an award rather than the parties reaching agreement; parties may agree on arbitral procedures but if they fail the Arbitration Act governs.
